Why Doing Less Has Become Raoul's Investment Strategy

When we first spoke more than two years ago, Raoul was anticipating the arrival of the "Banana Zone," a period of explosive crypto price appreciation driven by expanding liquidity. That rally never materialized as he expected, but his underlying investment philosophy has barely changed.

Over the past year, Raoul has made just two purchases during significant market corrections, alongside adding a position in $ZEC. Rather than actively trading market cycles, he focuses on accumulating assets he believes will appreciate over longer periods. His principle comes down to compounding and the psychological difficulty of timing the market. Selling near a market peak might sound straightforward, but buying back after prices fall is considerably harder since investors are likely to hesitate, expect prices to decline further, and eventually find themselves watching prices recover from the sidelines.

Raoul uses deviations from long-term logarithmic price trends to identify moments when assets are particularly undervalued. Buying at depressed prices, such as accumulating Solana and Ethereum during the 2022 downturn, helped his portfolio recover to previous highs before the broader market did.

Raoul acknowledges that the relationship between global liquidity and cryptocurrency prices has been weaker than he anticipated, as a disproportionate share of available capital has flowed into AI-related technology stocks. Thank you for this, @_NathanCalvin. I appreciate and am a fan of the investigative work you’ve done on behalf of AI safety and believe your comments are coming from a constructive, honest place, and that it benefits the public to have people whose job is to scrutinize the actions of frontier AI companies. I think something would be wrong if companies of the size of Anthropic didn’t get harshly criticized basically every day; strong antibodies against corporate power are a healthy feature of a free society, and especially so when issues of the gravity of the one we’re facing are at play. I also do agree that some of the examples you cite were mistakes by Anthropic.

That said, I disagree with the thrust of your post. At the core, a good fraction of the things you criticize are consequences of Anthropic’s basic theory of change that we have held for many years. Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the “race to the top” — by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.

I believe that if we take a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us, they far outweigh the list you’ve made, while at the same time I also disagree with some of the items on your list. Here are some things Anthropic has done, in the same period you’ve cited (the last year), which were very costly to us commercially while having strong safety benefits:

1. We played a key role in SB53 (and other state laws), at a time when doing so was politically perilous to the company and AI regulation was very unpopular. We in fact argued for a stronger version of SB53 than was ultimately passed; there were a lot of stakeholders and we were not the limiting factor in the strength of the bill that was passed.

2. We have very strong biological safeguards on our models, because we’ve seen concerning results in bio uplift trials and even seen and blocked potential attempts to misuse our models for bioweapons (as seen in our threat intelligence report from a few weeks ago). This is a very serious threat that we want to have zero tolerance for. But having very low false negatives means having significant false positives (despite months of effort on our part to improve the classifiers), enough so that biologists joke about how restrictive our classifiers are, and competitors sometimes sell against us by touting their more permissive bio capabilities. This has been very painful to us in an area where we care a lot about supporting an ecosystem of Claude users (biomedical science; and it is particularly frustrating to me as a biologist), but it’s the right thing to do and we intend to keep doing it.

quoted.text:
One of the great coincidences in finance:

In 1952 Harry Markowitz published "Portfolio Selection." It became the foundation of modern asset management. The idea is that you optimize a diversified basket of assets along an efficient frontier by claiming to know what the currently “efficient” part of the frontier is (even though no one actually knows which assets will perform most efficiently in the future). 

That same year a British actuary named Frank Redington published "Review of the Principles of Life-Office Valuations." It showed how institutions could immunize their liabilities by matching them with assets across time. It became the foundation of institutional asset-liability matching. Almost nobody outside of insurance and banking knows it.

The interesting thing is institutions adopted Redington because matching assets to liabilities is just the sensible way to manage cash flows. Meanwhile the industry sold Markowitz to retail investors….

quoted.text:
The premise for why static support/resistance levels "work" is that traders who bought or sold at those levels will exhibit that behavior again when they see the price get back to that important level. If it was a good place to buy before, it will be a good place to buy again in the future, or so goes the thinking. 

Now ask yourself, does anyone make trading decisions regarding IWM based on a price level they remember from months ago? 

And furthermore, since IWM is based on the Russell 2000 Index, does it make sense that the outcome of those stocks aggregated together into an index would be driven by this supposed effect of seeing a prior ETF level get reached again, and trading based on it?

The supposed effects of static support and resistance behavior break down when stocks are pooled into an index or ETF, especially one that is not greatly watched by people. IWM arguably is watched more than many ETFs, but the breakdown effect is the same. A level seen months ago is just not that important to what happens now.

IF YOU DOUBT ME, and I am confident many readers will, try this: Pull up a chart of IWM, and start drawing horizontal lines from any prior tops or bottoms months ago which you think were important. Then see how many of those levels really mattered to future price action. But you should only do this if you are ready to have your preconceived notions get challenged by evidence.

Then try it with other small ETFs. Try it with commodity prices. Try it with currencies

MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: Despite a wave of Iranian attacks since the beginning of October, total Middle Eastern crude oil flows (ex-Iran) remain resilient. Flows are becoming, however, lumpier (days of multiple tanker crossings followed by days of very few tankers). 

Overall, Middle East (ex-Iran) crude flows, including Strait of Hormuz plus all the bypass routes, are holding at ~75% of pre-war levels, down from a ~95% *peak* in the last days of September. Crucially, despite the drop in recent days, the Oct 1-Oct 10 period average remains above Sep full month average (and well above full month August). Kuwait is struggling the most right now. UAE, Iraq and KSA (the last one using both Persian Gulf and Red Sea) are doing relatively well.

All said, the risk is to the downside if the Iranian attacks continue (and if they become more successful). Iran has sunk at least one container ship in the SoH over the last 24 hours. The same goes for Red Sea flows under Houthi / Iraq militias potential attacks. For Iran itself, Hormuz remains closed.

One key indicator to follow: despite the Iranian attacks against SoH traffic, the physical premium for Middle Eastern crude has come down significantly in recent days, touching today a near 2½-month low.

This superb @RealAlpineMacro chart, titled "The French Disease," shows just how gigantic the gap is that AI has to close.

France is an aging, uncompetitive, highly indebted, and politically polarized nation, where government spending accounts for a whopping 58% of GDP.

Meanwhile, productivity growth, arguably the only painless way out of mounting government debt and persistent budget deficits, has collapsed to virtually zero.

This is another excellent illustration of France's vulnerability within the Eurozone and why expectations for AI are so high.

Can AI close the gap? Partly, surely. But the divergence between government spending and productivity growth has become so extreme that additional measures will almost certainly be needed to prevent a debt crisis. If not now, then later.

I think most investors recognize these risks. But recognizing them is one thing. Actually adjusting your portfolio is another.
